title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
gist: UCSD and Oberlin researchers built a sub-$100, coin-sized Wi-Fi implant that installs in about 15 seconds through an unlocked exterior hatch on a Boeing 737 and can override the Flight Management Computer's waypoints and takeoff variables while spoofing the pilot's display. Boeing, briefed since spring 2020, says existing layers of protection sufficiently limit real-world risk and has not told the researchers of any technical fix, which they expect could take years given how rarely commercial aircraft are redesigned.

themes.theme: The attack: cost, access, and capability

insights.claim: A coin-sized Wi-Fi-enabled hardware implant costing less than $100 can be fitted in under a minute into a Boeing 737 port reachable through an exterior hatch that maintenance workers and airport staff routinely access between flights.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Sub-$100 hardware cost plus 60-second installation puts a credible aviation attack within reach of many more actors than bomb-based threats, shifting the aviation security spend toward ground-access controls.

insights.claim: The targeted port can be reached with no special tools in about 15 seconds and is typically protected by only a hatch without a lock, with the device hidden entirely from view under the dust cap that normally covers the connector.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Physical concealment plus no-lock access means routine visual inspection would not detect an installed implant, so mitigation must be design-level, not procedural.

insights.claim: The implant works by sending electrical signals at a higher current than legitimate ones on the bus connecting the Flight Management Computer and the Multipurpose Control Display Unit, letting it override real commands, a technique the researchers dubbed Bus Driver.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: The vulnerability is electrical rather than software, so it cannot be patched by a firmware update and requires hardware isolation or cryptographic authentication to fix.

themes.theme: Consequence modeling and residual pilot defenses

insights.claim: Falsifying outside air temperature or aircraft load can prevent a 737 from reaching the necessary speed for takeoff before running out of runway, making takeoff-calculation tampering as dangerous as navigation tampering.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Attacks on input data rather than control surfaces are harder to detect and defend, a threat pattern that generalizes to any system where operators trust computed values.

insights.claim: Flight-plan tampering could route a plane into another country's airspace where it could be commandeered by that country's air force, crash it into a mountain, or send a transoceanic flight in the wrong direction until it ran out of fuel over water.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: The geopolitical escalation path, forcing an aircraft into hostile airspace, is the scenario that would draw state-level attention and funding to this class of vulnerability.

themes.theme: Boeing's response and the remediation timeline

insights.claim: Boeing reviewed its component designs, installations, and interfaces in response to the findings but says its technical experts are confident that existing layers of protection provide sufficient mitigation to significantly limit the feasibility and risk of real-world attacks.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A manufacturer publicly declining to acknowledge exploitable risk is the precondition for regulatory intervention if any incident later occurs, a latent liability marker.
insights.quote: Our technical experts are confident that the layers of protection in place on the airplane, including within the system design and the operating environment, provide sufficient mitigation to significantly limit the feasibility and risk of real-world attacks,
insights.locator: When WIRED reached out to Boeing

insights.claim: Boeing has not told the researchers about any technical fix for the vulnerabilities despite disclosures beginning more than six years ago, and they speculate no update may be implemented for years given how rarely commercial airplanes are redesigned.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Aircraft redesign cycles measured in decades mean disclosed avionics vulnerabilities persist far longer than in any other computing sector, a structural difference that should reshape aviation threat models.

insights.claim: The researchers explicitly state in their paper that all of the authors routinely travel on Boeing 737 aircraft and expect to continue doing so, framing the finding as a planning problem rather than grounds for grounding aircraft.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Explicit non-alarmism from the discoverers limits near-term consumer and airline reaction, so any market impact will come through procurement and regulation, not demand.

insights.claim: The researchers' simplest proposed fixes are to plug the port with epoxy or remove it altogether, with longer-term options including software detection of Bus Driver, better electrical isolation as used in some military aircraft, and cryptographic authentication of signals between plane systems.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A near-zero-cost physical mitigation exists, so failure to apply it becomes an accountability question rather than an engineering one, and the long-term fixes point to a retrofit market in avionics authentication.

insights.claim: The generalizable lesson is that threat models for any highly sensitive system must be revised as attacker technology advances, because 20th-century threat models rarely survive contact with 21st-century tools and techniques.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for assessing legacy critical infrastructure: assume any air-gapped or physically-secured assumption made before cheap Wi-Fi SoCs is now obsolete.
